newsitem.title: USA: U.S. deports record numbers last year.
newsitem.headline: U.S. deports record numbers last year.

text.p: The U.S. Immigration and Naturalisation Service (INS) said on Tuesday it deported a record 67,000 illegal immigrants in fiscal year 1996, a 34 percent increase over 1995.

INS Commissioner Doris Meissner told a news conference the increase reflected "the Clinton administration's determination to remove criminal aliens and other deportable aliens from the United States."

She cited statistics showing that since the Clinton administration took office, more than 160,000 illegal aliens have been deported. Three out of four of those deported were Mexican, with most of the rest coming from other Latin American or Caribbean nations.

Republican presidential candidate Bob Dole has been highly critical of President Bill Clinton for not cracking down hard enough on illegal immigration, a central issue in the key border states of Texas and California.
The Clinton administration leaked the INS year-end figures to the Los Angeles Times earlier this week while Dole was hammering away at the immigration issue while campaiging in California.
But the numbers of deported are a small percentage of the illegal aliens in the United States, according to independent analysts, even though the estimates vary widely.
The Policy Institute of California, for example, said that between 1.3 million to 2.2 million of the total 6 million new residents in the state in the 1980s were illegal aliens.

An INS official, speaking anonymously, said that the latest expulsion figures were a drop in the bucket. "If we had the manpower, we could deport 1,800 a month from the Los Angeles County jail system alone, 22,000 a year from one jail alone," he said.

Meissner predicted that deportations would continue to rise, partly because of an INS programme that identifies and processes for deportation criminal aliens serving sentences in state and federal prisons.
Republicans have complained that the Clinton administration has allowed people with criminal records to obtain citizenship, but Meissner disputed the claim.
